title: Chapter 91 — Floor Metrics That Actually Matter
intro: A KPI is not the problem. A KPI is evidence that points toward a problem. This chapter teaches you how to measure what matters — and how to stop building metrics that reward people for gaming the system.

sections.title: Traffic Is Not What You Think It Is
sections.content:
Traffic is one of the most important retail KPIs. It is also one of the most misunderstood and manipulated.

A traffic counter measures movement through the door. A salesperson measures customer opportunities. These are not the same thing.

Modern stores use door sensors, AI cameras, security systems, heat mapping, Wi-Fi tracking, and video analytics. These provide total store traffic. The problem is that traffic does not equal buying opportunities.

A family of six shopping together registers as six on the counter but represents one buying group. A couple is two people but one opportunity. A customer returning merchandise, a delivery pickup, a parts purchase, an employee entering, a vendor entering — every one of these changes the count without representing a sale opportunity.

sections.title: Buying Groups — The Real Metric
sections.content:
The real metric is not people. It is buying groups.

One customer shopping alone equals one buying group. A husband and wife equals one buying group. A family of five buying a kitchen equals one buying group.

The door counter might say five people. The reality is one buying opportunity.

This distinction is critical for every metric that follows — closing ratio, conversion rate, staffing, and marketing ROI. If you are measuring against the wrong denominator, every conclusion you draw is wrong.

sections.title: Why Salespeople Underreport Ups
sections.content:
Many stores ask salespeople to record every customer they assist. In reality, this is often inaccurate because salespeople have incentives to manipulate the numbers.

Reason one — protecting closing percentage. The formula is simple: closing ratio equals sales divided by ups. If a salesperson records fewer ups while maintaining the same sales volume, their closing percentage increases. They appear to be a stronger salesperson.

Reason two — gaming the rotation system. Many retailers use an up rotation: Salesperson 1, then 2, then 3, then 4, then repeat. If someone convinces the team that a customer was not really an up, they move to the next rotation faster. That increases their odds of receiving the next qualified buyer.

Common excuses include: 'They were just looking.' 'They only needed a repair part.' 'They were waiting for someone.' Some of these are legitimate. Many are not.

The KPI is now influencing behavior instead of measuring behavior. That is a problem.

sections.title: The Two-System Solution
sections.content:
The best practice is to use two independent measurements and compare them.

System 1 — Traffic Counter. Measures total traffic, store trends, marketing effectiveness, and seasonal volume.

System 2 — Salesperson Self-Recorded Ups. Measures individual opportunities, closing ratio, and conversion performance.

When you compare both, they reveal additional intelligence. Example: the traffic counter shows 120 people. The sales team recorded 94 buying groups. The difference is 26 percent. That tells management roughly one quarter of traffic consists of non-buying visitors or additional family members.

That percentage becomes a benchmark. If it suddenly changes significantly, management should investigate why. Neither metric is correct by itself. Traffic counters over-count. Salespeople often under-count. The truth is usually found by comparing both over time. The objective is not perfect accuracy. It is consistency.

sections.title: Closing Percentage — What Is Good?
sections.content:
The industry averages for closing percentage vary by retail format. Big box retail typically runs 18 to 25 percent. Specialty retail runs 25 to 30 percent.

I think these numbers are low. I believe they create a culture where mediocre performance is considered acceptable because it matches the average.

My expectations are higher. For specialty retail, I target 40 to 50 percent. Exceptional stores should reach 60 percent or higher. For big box, at minimum one in four customers should be buying — 25 percent as a floor, not a ceiling.

Why? Because specialty retailers generally offer multiple brands, broad selection, expert knowledge, financing, delivery, installation, and professional staff. If the customer leaves without buying, the question is usually not 'did we have the right brand?' It is 'why did they choose to buy somewhere else?'

In most specialty environments, the products are available from multiple competitors. The competitive advantage becomes the salesperson, the experience, the trust, the value, the relationship, and the process.

sections.title: Averages Are Not Goals
sections.content:
One of the biggest mistakes organizations make is treating industry averages as success. An average simply describes current performance across the industry. It does not define what your business is capable of achieving.

Do not compete against the industry average. Compete against your own best performance. That is the mindset that separates management from leadership.

If you reach 40 percent, the question is whether you can reach 45. Then 50. Then 60. You never stop because customer acquisition is expensive and every additional percentage point of conversion increases the return on every marketing dollar already being spent.

Example: Store A has 100 buying groups and closes at 25 percent — 25 sales. Store B has 100 buying groups and closes at 40 percent — 40 sales. Without spending another dollar on advertising, Store B generates 60 percent more sales from the same traffic. Improving closing percentage is one of the highest-return investments a retailer can make.

sections.title: Never Build a KPI That Rewards Gaming
sections.content:
Here is a principle that every manager needs to hear: never build a KPI that rewards people for manipulating the metric instead of improving the outcome.

Good KPIs change behavior in the right direction. Bad KPIs teach employees how to win the numbers game while the business quietly loses.

If your closing ratio metric incentivizes salespeople to underreport ups, the metric is broken — not the people. If your rotation system incentivizes cherry-picking customers, the system is broken.

The goal is to measure behavior accurately so you can coach it. The moment a metric becomes something people manage instead of something that measures performance, it has stopped being useful.

Closing percentage is the outcome. The sales process is the cause. Improve the process — improve every step of the 10 Steps — and the KPI follows.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating floor metrics, ask:

Are ups being recorded honestly — or gamed?
Is management comparing traffic counter data against self-reported ups to spot discrepancies?
Is the team measuring buying groups or just bodies through the door?
Is closing percentage being used as a coaching tool or a judgment weapon?
Is the store competing against its own best performance or just matching industry averages?
Do the KPIs incentivize the right behavior — or do they reward manipulation?

Managers should never weaponize closing percentages. Use them to ask better coaching questions: are we greeting effectively, discovering real needs, presenting enough options, building trust, handling objections properly, and asking for the sale?
